query: For refractory materials, experiments at the solid-to-fluid transition are difficult and yield sparse, scattered data, while the large compositional space of high-entropy systems makes systematic screening impractical. DFT free-energy studies can determine the transition from the crossing of solid and dense-fluid Gibbs energies and provide associated thermodynamic properties, but their reliance on extensive ab initio molecular dynamics makes them costly. TOR-TILD has shown high efficiency for elemental and binary systems, yet becomes substantially slower for multicomponent systems. Any broadly useful approach must retain ab initio-level accuracy, represent all thermodynamic effects identified as important, treat both phases around the transition, and remain practical across relevant compositions and temperatures. For a multicomponent high-entropy material in these high-temperature states, what single intervention could improve determination of transition temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change, and dense-fluid heat capacity? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and causal mechanism, its predicted outcome relative to existing experimental and computational baselines, its boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive experiment or benchmark that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The incorporation of longitudinal spin fluctuations (LSFs) in first-principles calculations will improve the determination of transition temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change, and dense-fluid heat capacity for multicomponent high-entropy materials.
generation.material_initial_state: Multicomponent high-entropy material in a solid state
generation.intervention: Incorporation of longitudinal spin fluctuations (LSFs) in first-principles calculations
generation.structural_mediator: Change in magnetic moments and entropy
generation.mechanism: LSFs induce sizable magnetic moments and alter partial contributions to free energy, leading to more accurate predictions of thermodynamic properties
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved accuracy in determining transition temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change, and dense-fluid heat capacity
generation.baseline: Existing experimental and computational methods without LSFs
generation.boundary: Applicability limited to high-entropy materials with complex magnetic interactions
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty in the accuracy of LSFs in predicting thermodynamic properties for all high-entropy materials

falsification_experiment.design: Comparison of predicted thermodynamic properties with experimental data for a high-entropy material
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the predicted values deviate significantly from experimental data, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Intervention effect. Base system: Polymorphic CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy in face-centered cubic (fcc) and hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structures. Intervention: Accounting for longitudinal spin fluctuations (LSFs) as a function of temperature in first-principles calculations. Processing: First-principles alloy theory using DFT with the LSF methodology (Dong et al.) and fluctuating medium approximation. Test conditions: Temperature range 50 K to 1200 K; volumes represented by Wigner-Seitz radius. Structure change: Finite magnetic moments thermally induced for Co, Cr, and Ni at all volumes even at 50 K; mean magnetic moments {m_I} exhibit monotonic dependency on volume and temperature. Property change: Magnetic moments for Co, Cr, and Ni increase with temperature; e.g., at 100 K, m_Co is 0.73 μ_B (fcc) and 0.67 μ_B (hcp); at 900 K, m_Co is 1.30 μ_B (fcc) and 1.27 μ_B (hcp). Mechanism: LSFs induce sizable magnetic moments for Co, Cr, and Ni, whereas Fe and Mn already have large spontaneous static magnetic moments. Evidence: simulated. Quote: "Accounting for the LSFs at finite temperature (contour plots in Fig. 1), finite magnetic moments have been thermally induced for Cr, Ni and C

Intervention effect. Base system: PM CoCrFeMnNi in fcc and hcp phases. Intervention: Calculation of fcc-hcp interfacial energy (σ) using the Olson and Cohen model and supercell approach. Processing: Comparison of σ derived from LSF and FS schemes with experimental lattice expansion. Test conditions: Temperature interval 300–900 K; extrapolation to 0 K. Structure change: LSFs slightly lower the interfacial energy σ compared to FS calculations. Property change: LSFs at finite temperature slightly lower σ by 0.5~0.7 mJ m^-2 in the temperature interval 300–900 K; σ predicted to be ~6.1 mJ m^-2 at 0 K in LSF vs 7.0 mJ m^-2 in FS. Mechanism: The role of LSFs disclosed in PM CoCrFeMnNi is in good agreement with that reported in PM γ-Fe and Fe-22.5 at.% Mn. Evidence: simulated. Quote: "It is evident from Fig. 4 that the LSFs at finite temperature slightly lower σ by 0.5~0.7 mJ m −2 in the temperature interval 300–900 K."

Intervention effect. Base system: PM CoCrFeMnNi. Intervention: Evaluation of magnetic moments {m_I} as a function of temperature with thermal lattice expansion. Processing: LSF calculations combined with experimental thermal lattice expansion data. Test conditions: Temperatures 100 K, 300 K, and 900 K. Structure change: Mean magnetic moments {m_I} in both phases significantly increase with temperature. Property change: At 100 K, difference in m_I between fcc and hcp phases amounts to ~0.05, 0.03, 0.17, and 0.23 μ_B for Co, Cr, Fe, and Mn respectively. Mechanism: The m_I of Fe and Mn shows more pronounced dependency on volume with respect to that on temperature, whereas LSFs give the prevailing contribution to the m_I of Co, Cr and Ni. Evidence: simulated. Quote: "It is evident that { m I } in both phases significantly increase with temperature, and at the given temperatures the magnetic states of the alloy components in the fcc phase are very close to those in the hcp phase."
